meta.subtitle: Cash-generative but still shrinking: at $2.25 the shares price in more than Expensify's guided free cash flow supports

analystCommentary: Expensify's Q2'26 10-Q shows a business whose reported revenue is still declining while it generates cash. Free cash flow turned positive in FY24 after a negative FY23, as the Cash flow section shows; what is missing is top-line growth, which the income statement section covers. Management's case rests on New Expensify, a claim the Growth section weighs against the reported figures. At $2.25 the shares sit in the upper part of the $0.69 – $2.81 52-week range. Valued on the company's fiscal 2026 free cash flow guide and a filed share count, our scenario weighting lands below the current price by more than the SELL line allows, so we rate the stock SELL: guided cash flow supports the shares, but at a lower price than today's, and nothing reported yet justifies a higher multiple.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Expensify, Inc. sells a cloud-based expense management platform covering corporate cards, bill pay, invoicing and travel booking to individuals, small and midsized businesses and enterprises; it was founded in 2008 and is based in San Francisco. Per the 10-Q MD&A, revenue comes from subscription fees, charged on monthly active members and level of service, plus interchange on the Expensify Card, issued through The Bancorp Bank, N.A. on the Visa network. Cashback paid to cardholders is booked as contra revenue. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026 the MD&A reports an average of 640,000 paid members across an average of 45,700 companies. The company reports a single segment, and FY25 revenue was $142.1M.

thesis.body: The bull argument is that a profitable but shrinking Classic product is funding a fast-growing New Expensify. The bear argument is that consolidated revenue is still falling and the consensus path in Growth offers no recovery. We lean to the bear side on price rather than on the business. Cash generation and the Q2 share reduction give the equity real support. Against that, paid members are declining and gross margin is compressing as card cashback rises. Until reported revenue shows the new-customer growth, we see the price as above what the guided free cash flow supports.

catalysts: Evidence in reported revenue that New Expensify growth is offsetting the Classic decline (see Growth).
Delivery against the fiscal 2026 free cash flow guidance (see Cash flow).
Any new repurchase authorization, which the earnings release does not announce (see Capital allocation).
risks: Subscription revenue and paid members keep falling as the Classic base shrinks (see Durability and Risks).
Card cashback starts rising by more dollars than interchange, narrowing the card's contribution to net revenue (see Risks).
A multi-class structure, with all LT10 and LT50 shares held in a Voting Trust, limits outside holders' influence (see Governance).

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue, net fell 5% in Q2'26 to $33.9M, which the 10-Q MD&A attributes to lower billable activity across the user base and higher contra revenue from Expensify Card cashback, partly offset by higher interchange. Subscription revenue was $30.8 million against $32.9 million a year earlier. Interchange revenue rose to $5.9 million from $5.3 million, but the cost of cashback rewards, booked as contra revenue, rose to $3.0 million from $2.5 million. Card adoption therefore adds interchange and contra revenue together, so the card program does less for net revenue than the interchange line alone suggests; this is the mechanism other sections refer back to. Gross margin fell to 48% from 52%; the MD&A cites the revenue factors above and higher amortization of capitalized software, partly offset by savings from using AI in place of human agents. Separately, Visa volume incentives, which reduce cost of revenue, were $0.2 million against $0.8 million. In thousands of dollars, the MD&A table shows sales and marketing of 4,677 in Q2'26, down from 14,346 a year earlier. For the six months it was 8,438, down from 17,888. Read together, the year-over-year fall in operating expenses comes from an unusually large prior-year second quarter rather than from a lower run-rate, and the excerpt is truncated before the MD&A explains it. The narrower loss from operations, 2,921 against 10,338, is therefore mostly a base effect. Net loss narrowed to $3.9 million from $8.8 million. The earnings release also reports non-GAAP net income of $3.4 million and Adjusted EBITDA of $6.6 million; non-GAAP net income differs from the GAAP net loss by stock-based compensation, which was 7,211 in the quarter. The underlying cost base is roughly flat while revenue is falling, so the quarter's improvement in the loss line should not be extrapolated.
financials.balanceCommentary: The vendor balance sheet table rounds to $0.1B, which is too coarse to track Expensify's year-to-year changes, and the excerpts available do not state a quarter-end cash balance. The vendor table also leaves FY25 total debt and net debt blank, so the debt position at year-end cannot be confirmed from these figures; earlier years show small debt balances at that rounding. Liquidity is the clearer signal: the current ratio was 3.30 at FY25 and 3.50 on a trailing basis. In thousands of dollars, other income, which the 10-Q MD&A says consists primarily of interest income, fell to 202 in Q2'26 from 889, and the excerpt does not give the cause. The gap in that picture is that, without a quarter-end cash figure, the cash effect of the Q2 repurchases cannot be measured. On balance we see adequate liquidity on the current ratios, with the caveat that the debt and cash lines are not confirmed.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash flow is the main support for the shares, but the record is shorter than it first looks. The vendor's FCF margin was negative in FY21 at -1.5% and in FY23 at -3.8%, and positive in FY22 at 18.1%, FY24 at 11.7% and FY25 at 11.6%, so steady cash generation dates from FY24. FY25 free cash flow was $16.5M on the vendor's definition, even though operating margin was -12.7%. The trailing FCF yield of 4.0% points to less free cash flow over the last twelve months than in FY25 on the same vendor basis, and the excerpts do not explain the gap. The earnings release reports $8.4 million of cash from operating activities and $6.4 million of free cash flow in Q2'26, and guides fiscal 2026 free cash flow to $12.0 million to $14.0 million. The company's measure differs from the vendor's: the release defines free cash flow as net cash provided by operating activities excluding changes in settlement assets, net and settlement liabilities, reduced by purchases of property and equipment and software development costs. We therefore do not compare the guide with the vendor's figures. Within the company's own measure, Q2 alone is large against the full-year guide, which implies either a weaker second half or conservative guidance; the release does not say which. Stock-based compensation, guided at $5.4 million to $7.4 million for Q3 2026 and driven primarily by pre-IPO RSUs with approximately three years of vesting remaining, is a real cost to holders that free cash flow does not capture: on the company's own guides, four quarters of it at the low end exceed a full year of free cash flow at the top end. We treat the guide as the anchor for our value rather than as a source of upside.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing GAAP earnings the stock is loss-making, with a P/E of -14.1x, so earnings multiples rest on forecasts. Consensus EPS is $0.12 for FY26E and $0.10 for FY27E, which puts the stock at 18.8x NTM earnings and ~22.5x FY27E. The vendor does not state whether consensus EPS is GAAP or adjusted; because Q2'26 combined a GAAP net loss with positive non-GAAP net income, we read consensus as closer to the non-GAAP basis. On sales the stock trades at 1.5x P/S. A high-teens forward multiple on EPS estimates that decline from FY26E to FY27E is not cheap for a company with no reported revenue growth, and an earnings multiple held at today's level would simply return today's price, so our scenarios value the shares on the company's free cash flow guide instead. The Street is more positive: the consensus target of $2.83 sits above the price, with one Buy and two Holds among three analysts.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: New Expensify growth shows up in consolidated revenue and paid members stabilize, so the market pays for growth; the stock reaches $3.00, the top of the Street target range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue tracks consensus (see Growth) and fiscal 2026 free cash flow lands within the $12.0 million to $14.0 million guide; at 15x the midpoint of that guide, a multiple we assume for a business whose consensus revenue is lower in FY26E and flat in FY27E, with EPS lower in FY27E, on the 10-Q's Q2'26 weighted average of 95,441,380 shares, the stock is worth $2.04.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The Classic decline runs ahead of consensus and free cash flow comes in at the low end of the guide while revenue keeps falling; at 12x, a lower multiple we assume because cash flow at the bottom of the guide, with stock-based compensation running above it (see Cash flow), gives no reason to pay the Base multiple, the stock is worth $1.51 on the same share count.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The page carries more than one share count, and the Base and Bear depend on it. The Quote line's ~91.19M is derived from the vendor's market cap, not filed. The filings point higher: the proxy's three share classes as of March 27, 2026, less the approximately 6.8 million shares repurchased in Q2, and the 10-Q's weighted average for the quarter both sit above the vendor figure. We use the 10-Q weighted average because it is a filed count for the quarter itself; it somewhat overstates the quarter-end count because the tender came during the quarter, while RSU vesting since March works the other way. The 15x Base multiple is a judgment, and it decides the label. A higher multiple is defensible: the Street targets noted above sit above the price, and no scenario gives separate credit for cash, which the pack does not state at quarter end and which would raise all three. A lower one is defensible too: the stock-based compensation described in Cash flow is a cost the guide does not deduct. We take that multiple as the middle of those arguments. We weight the Base at 50% because the guide was issued in August with half the year already reported. We put 30% on Bear, more than on Bull, because the Bear driver needs one thing to go wrong, a faster Classic decline, while the Bull driver needs reported revenue to turn and the market to pay for it. Bull carries 20%. Valuing the Base one turn higher would derive HOLD; moving ten points of weight from Bear to Base would not. The $1.80–$2.20 target range brackets the Base: the low end reaches a little under halfway from the Base toward the Bear, because the Bear carries real weight, and the high end stays below the price because only the Bull sits above it.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Expensify reports a single segment, with FY25 revenue of $142.1M. Within it, the 10-Q MD&A splits revenue sources into subscription fees and Expensify Card interchange, with cashback netted against revenue. The CEO's shareholder letter describes two products, Expensify Classic and New Expensify, that share servers, code, team and customers; the company does not report them as segments, and the Growth section weighs the one metric management gives for the newer product.

moatFactors.name: Installed base and workflow integration
moatFactors.body: The MD&A reports over 15 million members added since founding and 1.9 billion expense transactions processed as of June 30, 2026, and the platform exports into third-party systems. That history supports cash flow. But the earnings release reports paid members down 2% year over year in Q2'26. The MD&A says month-to-month arrangements can be terminated by either party without penalty, while annual subscribers who leave early must pay the remaining obligation plus any fees; the excerpt does not give the mix between the two, so we credit the base with only limited lock-in.

moatFactors.name: Expensify Card
moatFactors.body: Card spend ties customers' daily transactions to the platform, which raises the cost of leaving more than a subscription alone does. The cost of that lock-in is economic rather than behavioral: as the income statement section shows, cashback offsets part of the interchange, so deeper lock-in comes at a price in net revenue.

moatFactors.name: Pricing
moatFactors.body: The FY25 10-K risk factors name pricing pressure from competition as a possible source of fluctuation in results. Gross margin slid to 50.3% in FY25 from 62.4% in FY21, but the 10-Q MD&A attributes the recent decline to cashback contra revenue and software amortization, so the series does not isolate pricing. We give no credit for pricing power because the figures available cannot show it either way.

businessMoat.durability: We see no durable moat today. Expensify's cash generation comes from an installed Classic base that the CEO describes in the shareholder letter as a fixed pool that will naturally drain, and an advantage that shrinks by design is not a moat. A moat could form if New Expensify scales and the card program deepens customer reliance, but neither shows yet in consolidated revenue.

points: The growth case rests on New Expensify. In the Q2 shareholder letter, the CEO says revenue from net new customers, who have never used Classic, grew by over 250% year over year to over $10 million ARR across over 10,000 new customers. This is a management-defined metric in the earnings release, not a figure reported in the 10-Q, and it is not reconciled to revenue, so we treat it as management's framing.

Consensus does not yet reflect it: FY26E revenue of ~$135.9M and FY27E revenue of $136.1M imply a lower year than FY25 followed by a flat one. Until New Expensify is large enough to move reported revenue, the Classic decline described in the income statement section dominates.

The Expensify Card is the reported growth line, with interchange revenue up 12% year over year in Q2'26 per the earnings release; the income statement section explains why net card contribution grows more slowly.

Product investment continues. The earnings release lists AI-powered workflow agents entering beta, the launch of the Expensify MCP, and 30+ product improvements in Q2. None of these has a disclosed revenue contribution, so we treat them as options rather than inputs to our estimates.

The CEO points to a large untapped market, citing 300 million businesses worldwide, of which he says less than 1% has ever paid for an expense tool. He says the path back to sustained growth depends on migrating remaining Classic customers onto New Expensify and scaling self-service acquisition; the market estimate is his, and nothing reported yet shows the conversion.

management.leadership: David Barrett is Founder and CEO and signs the shareholder letter in the Q2'26 earnings release. The letter is candid that Classic is a shrinking base. It is also promotional: it calls Q2 "the most exciting quarter in years" and says either of the two products alone "should be reasonably valued higher than the current business is being today." We give credit for the candor about Classic and discount the valuation claim, which the reported figures do not yet support.
management.capitalAllocation: In Q2'26 the company ran a modified Dutch auction tender offer seeking to repurchase $25 million of Class A stock and bought 6.1 million shares at $1.20 per share; the earnings release says the tender was substantially undersubscribed. It then repurchased approximately 0.7 million additional shares at an average price of $1.63, for a total of approximately 6.8 million shares, which the company describes as an approximately 7% reduction in shares outstanding. FY25 share repurchases were $9.1M. Buying back stock well below today's price was good for remaining holders. Against that, ongoing stock-based compensation from pre-IPO RSUs works against the reduction over time, and the release does not say whether further buybacks are planned.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement filed April 10, 2026, the Executive Committee, acting for the Board, determined that Mr. Christen, Ms. Liu and Ms. Pao are independent directors under Exchange Act and Nasdaq rules; the excerpt does not state the total board size. The Executive Committee also identifies and nominates director candidates, and the company has no formal board diversity policy. All LT10 and LT50 shares are held by the Expensify Voting Trust, which held 83.6% of voting power as of March 27, 2026, under an agreement intended to keep decision-making centered on employees. All of the proxy's ownership percentages predate the Q2 repurchase, which reduced Class A shares outstanding and so shifts these percentages. The related-party disclosures are employment arrangements with Mr. Alvarez Divo, Mr. Mills and Mr. Vidal, each of whom also holds LT10 and LT50 shares, which sit in the Voting Trust, and voting power per the proxy table of 2.0%, 6.6% and 1.8% respectively, so they are inside the bloc that controls the vote.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 27, 2026, per the proxy, David Barrett held 3.1% of Class A shares and 36.7% of voting power, and all current executive officers and directors as a group (8 persons) held 5.7% of Class A shares and 48.9% of voting power. Their holdings include LT10 and LT50 shares, which sit in the Voting Trust, and it is the trust's control of the vote, described in Governance, that leaves outside Class A holders unable to change the board or block strategy. Their economic stake in Class A is small relative to that control, so outside holders rely on management's alignment rather than on voting rights; this is the central governance tension. Holders of more than five percent of Class A include Steve McLaughlin at 11.2% and Octopus Head Inc. at 7.3%.

idiosyncratic: Classic attrition: the decline described in Durability continues. Watch paid members and subscription revenue in the next 10-Q for whether New Expensify is offsetting it.

Card economics: in Q2'26 cashback grew faster than interchange in percentage terms, but interchange still rose by more dollars, so the card added to net revenue. If cashback starts rising by more dollars than interchange, the card's net contribution would narrow and could eventually reverse. Watch the gap between interchange revenue and the cost of cashback rewards.
Partner dependence: the card program runs under an agreement with The Bancorp Bank, N.A. on the Visa network, so any change to that arrangement would affect interchange revenue.
Result volatility: the FY25 10-K risk factors, filed February 26, 2026, warn that quarterly and annual results have fluctuated significantly and may not meet investor or analyst expectations.
risks.systemic: The 10-Q MD&A says the business depends on the overall state of the economy because the majority of customers are small and medium-sized businesses, and cites elevated inflation, tariff and trade issues, and geopolitical uncertainty including the conflict in the Middle East. Because revenue is billed on active members and card spend, a slowdown in hiring or business travel would show up quickly. The same risk factors separately list declines in foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar as a source of fluctuation in results.

body: We rate Expensify SELL with a $1.80–$2.20 target range. On the free cash flow guide and the filed share count, our weighted value sits below the price by more than the SELL line allows, and the label rests on the Base multiple argued in Valuation. A modest fall in the price would derive HOLD on the same scenarios. What would move us to HOLD is free cash flow tracking toward the top of the guide alongside evidence in reported revenue that New Expensify is outgrowing the Classic decline. A miss against the guide would fall below our Bear and widen the downside.
